edits.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts a tall structure, traditionally described as a raised building or viewing tower. One account treats Shang forms without the lower 口 as the initial form and says the graph was later standardized; it does not establish separate original roles for 冂 and 口. Another analysis treats 冂 as a raised foundation and the rest as a tower, with 口 either added later or representing a window. The original construction remains unsettled.

Examples are labeled Shang, Western Zhou, Spring and Autumn, Warring States, small-seal, Han, and Han clerical or regular scripts. One account describes early Shang forms without the lower 口 as the initial form, followed by similar Zhou forms and later abbreviations and standardization. Detailed changes between individual forms are not established.

Shang oracle-bone and Zhou bronze examples are reported in which 高祖 is interpreted as “remote ancestor.” These reports support a historical use, but the cited inscription contexts have not been independently verified here.

Dictionary records and textual citations attest these uses, but do not establish when they arose or how they developed from “high” or “tall.” Separate reports describe uses for “distant” and later uses for vertical height and “high” in the high/low sense; they do not settle a single semantic pathway.

The traditional account links the tall-building picture to “high,” but no verified inscription context securely establishes the earliest lexical sense or the chronology of that connection. Reports describe “distant” uses before Spring and Autumn and Warring States uses for height; the pathway between these meanings remains unresolved.
